en: Ignorance alone, conjoined with consciousness, is the single cause of the world;
the one witness of the mind thus knows the three worlds. (1)
With an intellect endowed with discernment, I know the Self as non-dual;
nevertheless, the conventional usage of bondage, liberation, and so forth is still perceived. || 2 ||
"Even though this phenomenal world is a mere illusory manifestation (vivarta) for me, it always appears as if real;
bound by this noose of doubt, please sever my uncertainty. (3)
Having heard these words of the disciple, the Guru spoke this clear reply:
"There is neither ignorance nor intellect, neither the world nor the state of being a witness. (4)
All things, such as fragrance and liberation, are established within You, the non-dual Reality;
when it is said that "the entire world appears," that world must be of the nature of Being, which is Brahman. (5)
Just as the reality of the rope persists even when [the snake] appears, so too the reality of Brahman alone exists as the substratum of the phenomenal world; that world does not truly exist. 6.
Just as sugar exists pervading the sugarcane,
so too are you pervading the three worlds in the form of the wondrous Brahman.
Just as all water in a desert is nothing but the desert itself, so too,
through profound inquiry, this entire triple world is seen to be pure consciousness alone.
All living beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are fashioned within you, just as modifications from bubbles to waves exist within the ocean. 9.
Just as the ocean certainly does not desire the state of being a wave,
so too you have no desire for the pleasures of the senses because of your nature as the Great Bliss.
Just as sugar, having pervaded flour, does not desire sweetness [separately], so too, when full bliss has pervaded the world, it does not desire that [worldly] bliss. 11.
Just as the desire for poverty does not exist for one who is prosperous, so too the desire for sense-objects cannot arise for you, who are immersed in the bliss of Brahman. 12.
Having seen both poison and nectar, the wise man abandons the poison;
likewise, having seen even the self, you should abandon the [false] self with diligence. 13.
The sun that illuminates a jar is not destroyed when the jar is destroyed;
likewise, the witness who illuminates the body is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. 14.
The entire world is formless, stainless, and of the nature of existence-consciousness;
since there is an absence of duality, tell me, how and from what source could fear arise for me, who am the Full? 15.
The entire world, beginning with the Brahman, is imagined within you, O Bliss;
the world is dissolved in you alone—tell me, how can you yourself be dissolved? 16.
For there is no manifold diversity, no collection of elements, nor sense organs, nor the group of vital breaths, nor the body;
there is no intellect, no mind, and no agent—the Brahman alone is the truth, the form of the Supreme Self. 17.
Know that all is happiness because of the destruction of great suffering, and all is of the nature of reality because of the destruction of the unreal;
it is indeed of the nature of consciousness, endowed with luminosity, and therefore the indivisible form of the Supreme Self. 18.

Consciousness alone is the body; consciousness alone is the worlds; consciousness alone is the elements; consciousness is the senses; consciousness is the agent; consciousness is the internal organ; consciousness alone is the truth, the nature of ultimate reality. 19.
I have no bondage, no liberation, no scripture, and no teacher;
for I am beyond duality, transcending illusion, while all this is but the play of illusion.
Let the wise man rule a kingdom or wander for alms without fear;
pure, he is not stained by faults, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Meritorious deeds and sinful actions performed in a dream do not persist upon waking;
likewise, O Lord, the meritorious and sinful actions performed while awake do not belong to me.
Let the body perform actions, or let speech be uttered here in vain;
let the intellect contemplate sovereignty—what loss is there for me, who am full? (23)
Let the vital breaths move according to their nature, or let the mind be struck down by desires;
how could there be suffering for me, who am filled with the nectar of bliss? 24.
This embodied soul, submerged in the ocean of bliss, is not perceived there,
just as salt situated within water has gone to dissolution therein.
The senses, the mind, the vital breaths, and the ego—having abandoned their mutual dull associations—are submerged in me, the ocean of consciousness. 26.
I know my true self immediately; ignorance has fled.
Today my sense of agency is destroyed, and there is no longer anything to be done anywhere.
In the ocean of the nectar of consciousness, the foam of the mind has dissolved and reached its end; the restless waves of mental fluctuations have subsided.
How can there be suffering for me here, who am this one, ever-present, motionless, perfectly full, and a tranquil ocean of bliss? 28.
I am the form of bliss, indivisible consciousness; I am higher than the highest, the dense radiance of pure awareness.
Just as clouds do not touch the sky, so the sufferings of saṃsāra do not touch me. 29.
Endowed with bone, flesh, excrement, intestines, skin, and hair, the gross body is an eater of food; therefore, I am the pure mass of consciousness.
These [states] depend upon the gross body; they do not belong to me, who am distinct from the gross.
I am not the insentient subtle body (liṅga); I am of the nature of consciousness, non-dual. || 31 ||

Hunger, thirst, blindness, deafness, desire, anger, and all such [afflictions] reside in the subtle body (liṅgadeha) and affect it; they do not affect me, the Lord who am without a subtle body (aliṅga). 32.
In this context, it is said that beginningless ignorance itself is the causal body;
I am not even the causal body, for I am self-luminous and stainless.
The attributes of insentience, pleasure, and pain reside in the causal body;
they do not exist in me, who am eternal and whose nature is changeless.
"The Supreme Lord exists as distinct from the individual soul; whence then is your status as the Supreme Lord?"—such is the discourse of ignorant people, which shall now be examined. (35)
When these three—the substratum, the reflection of consciousness, and the intellect—appear as one due to ignorance, they are then called the "jīva. (36)
The substrate cannot be the individual soul (jīva), because each is immutable;
and since it is not a real entity, the reflection of consciousness has no status as a soul.

For each individual soul, there is no [separate] intellect because even the intellect is insentient; therefore, there must be a triad consisting of the individual soul, the reflected consciousness (ābhāsa), and the immutable intellect (kūṭastha-buddhi). || 38 ||
The appearance of Māyā, the Pure Self, and these three together constitute Maheśvara. Since the appearance of Māyā is insubstantial, it cannot individually be the Lord. || 39 ||
Because of his fullness, immutability, and purity, he is the Great Lord (Maheśvara);
however, due to the insentience of Māyā, lordship over it is indeed difficult to establish.
Therefore, this triad is false; its object cannot be God. Thus, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) appear due to one's own ignorance, for they do not exist in reality. 41.

Just as the space within a jar and the space within a hut are imagined within the great space, so too are the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) imagined within me, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). 42.
Upon the dissolution of illusion and its effects, there is neither lordship nor the state of being a limited soul;
therefore, I am pure consciousness alone, free from all adjuncts within the expanse of consciousness.

I always take refuge in the silence [of realization] that "I am That"—the state which is the mass of truth-consciousness, infinite, non-dual, devoid of all objects of perception, free from affliction, stainless, and auspicious. 44.

I take refuge in silence as that which is full, non-dual, indivisible consciousness, devoid of the conceptualization of universal diversity, and a portion of the peerless, supreme awareness—ever saying "I am That. 45.

Free from birth and death, pleasure and pain, and far removed from caste, policy, family, and lineage—the cause of this world which is an evolution of consciousness—I always take refuge in the silence of "I am That. 46.
Just as darkness is perceived by an owl in the light of the sun, so does darkness appear to the deluded man within the self-luminous supreme bliss. 47.
Just as one afflicted by the obstruction of vision thinks that the sun does not exist, so the embodied soul covered by ignorance thinks that Brahman does not exist. 48.

Just as nectar, being distinct from poison, is not tainted by the defects of poison, so too, being distinct from the insentient and manifesting its own luminosity, I am not touched by the defects of the insentient. 49.
Even a tiny spark of a lamp can destroy a vast darkness;
likewise, even a slight awakening can pacify great ignorance.
Because I am of the nature of consciousness, I have no insentience; because I am truth, I have no falsehood;
because I am bliss, I have no suffering. Yet, due to ignorance, that triad appears to me.
Just as a snake does not exist in a rope throughout the three periods of time, so too the world—from egoity down to the body—does not exist in me; I am non-dual.
Virtuous people do not accept that darkness exists within the sun because it is its very nature to illuminate;
yet, alas, my deluded intellect perceives that darkness as the witness of its own effects! 53.
Just as cold water becomes hot through contact with fire, so too does agency arise through the relation of identity with the intellect; yet in reality, it does not truly exist. 54.
The sky is not sprinkled by drops of water, nor is it purified by them;
likewise, this [Self] is not purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā, for it is eternally pure.
Just as a tree is never satiated by the fruits produced from itself,
so too there is no satiety for me through the food, drink, and other things projected upon me.
A thief imagined upon a post does not subvert the nature of that post;
likewise, a soul imagined within oneself cannot subvert one's own true nature. (57)
The wise declare that sleep is the dissolution of the intellect within ignorance;
how then could there be sleep in Me, wherein ignorance and its effects have dissolved? (58)
This full blossoming of the intellect is proclaimed as waking;
yet for me, no waking exists, because I am devoid of modification and the like.
The movement of the intellect within the subtle channels gives rise to dream;
likewise, in me, who am devoid of the property of movement, there is no dream.
For me, who am perfect, eternal, pure, and luminous, what need is there for bathing, since adventitious impurities do not exist? (61)
Since there is no country, where is there to go? Since there is no place, where can there be a stay?
In me, who am full and non-dual, place and country are merely imagined.
Verily, thirst arises from the drying up of the movement of the vital breaths; how can this arise in me, whose nature is consciousness and who am beyond all drying? 63.
When the channels are oppressed by wind and fire, hunger arises;
since those two are the causes of that oppression, how could it exist in me, whose nature is pure consciousness?
Decrepitude consists of the loosening of the body's stability and the appearance of white hair; that does not exist in me, who am partless and all-pervading.
Indeed, youth is surely characterized by intense pride within the pleasure of dalliance with women;
but in me, who am the supreme, full Self-bliss, there is truly no such thing as youth.
Childhood, pervaded by deluded intellect and always an abode of sufferings, ends in a disposition prone to anger; it is not for me, who am an ocean of the waters of happiness.
Thus, for those people who are always immersed in the ocean of inquiry into reality, the supreme non-dual realization becomes direct perception; of this there is no doubt. 68.

Thus ends the *Svātmaprakāśikā*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
